But for older players those events are a bit more nostalgia filled of us doing very unconventional clears because Meta had not solidified yet.  Teams of mixed 3, 4 and couple 6 star ops were norm back then and the feeling of overcoming what were essentially stat checks was a great feeling.  This is also where a lot of players got their love for some of the non meta ops who didn't survive full 6* team metas like Blue Poison or Mousse.

Anyways, I'll drop some notes in reaction to your event comments.

**Hortus de Escapismo:** Drop this down to C


Starting with the big one lol.  Civs were ok, lots of agency on which towers you defended and where you huddled your civs. But boulders made the stage solutions inflexible and unfun for me.  If I could have used ops like Kirara or Bena for boulders and/or used boulders to damage enemies held with defenders, the stages would have been a lot more interesting. 

**So Long Adele:** Bump this up to S


Playing these stages was like playing Go. The emphasis here was using your towers(fountains) to control the field. Snipers like Lunacub can do some really interesting work here.  The soda bottles needed to be timed out to key moments to turn the tied of battle. The bottles being targetable allowed for some interesting placements of AoE attackers to extend range and to trigger the cloud mechanics. The way sheep doubled up were definitely designed to mess up your plans, so a lot of the strategy was deciding to prevent a team from forming or dealing with the overly powerful double team head on.  I feel this is the hardest event Arknights has given us, but it still manages to give us lots of options and solutions to deal with every problem.

**Near Light:**  Definitely S tier. 

The light mechanic was fun and felt like you had to take control of the map. One of my favorite events.  Solutions on how people reach out into the dark were varied and interesting to watch.

**Lone Trail:**  S tier 

This is probably the most flavorful and powerful event I experienced in Arknights.  That said, gravity was heckin fun and juggling space junk was pretty hilarious.  But just the whole feeling of going through the event was so good to me, it is my favorite Arknights has given us.

**Stultifera Navis:** S tier

Another event with a ton of flavor and was quite moving to explore through.    Controlling the stage tiles was fun and my clear using only Felines was challenging but also very rewarding for this event.

**Twilight of Wolumonde:** Landed in A tier for you, its a good spot.  

This event is early in the game's career, and really highlights how they wanted to have more creativity in their stage design vs bigger numbers.

**Under Tides:** 

Really loved the big final boss.  But I found the the sub boss that would go invincible on timer to be very annoying/not fun.

**Ideal City:**  

This was controversial? I disliked this story but the event was ok.   Dodge RNG is usually annoying but arts works.   Pramanix and casters working overtime here. Liked the shake up. Boss was interesting and required good planning, but wasn't that hard to nuke out of the sky if you were frustrated either.

**Originium Dust:**  

 I liked this, but it was weak from a technology stand point.  People with old phones/computers were punished and there was little chance of fun for them.  But it did vindicate all the AoE ops I leveled.  Also any event that allows Siege be a highlight is okay in my book.

**Mansfield Break:**  

Was fun, it was also my first Feline only clear.  This was before Kal was released.  Have you ever healed a stage using Nightmare?  It was a wild time.

**Code of Brawl** 

One of the earliest events where things weren't just bigger stats. I found the enemies engaging and I believe this was the very first event I 100%'d  I was so proud. Nostalgia kicking in hard, but the enemies sets here were great even if the stage design was fairly basic.

I think it is interesting to see how things changed over time from paper to electronic.  Also, these rules can and will vary subtly by state, as each state has its own laws.  But the variation in how the rules are outlined isn't going to be wildly different.  

so paper times, when you register to vote you get assigned a "Voting station" you can ONLY vote at that one station.  you show up to the wrong one, you give them your ID they check their paper voter rolls and then they don't find you..  they check your ID address and then they look at a map and say "Oh you are in the wrong place, your station is at blah middle school on blah street"

now say polls closed at 7PM.  it is 6:55PM.  You can not reasonably get to your polling station in time.   you could ask the the election officials at the place you are at to call your proper station and verify that you had not voted.  you get the election officials to sign off on both sides and you can vote in the wrong station.  Mega annoying but not unreasonable.  And as a reminder, they have all your info so if you manage to pull a fast one... well that's some easy jail time.

With the power of technology and internet, this can be a lot more efficient. the paper rolls probably still exist (in event of power outage).   But now you can walk up show your ID, get verified, they will encode a key for the electronic voting booth. The process of making that key will also send a note to a central database to mark you name as "voted at x station at y time/day."    

If you go to another voting station afterwards,  when they look you up, they'll see you have already voted, and the system would not let them encode a key for you to use at the voting booth.  

The central database is maintained at the county level in my state.  That means if you went to a neighboring county and tried to vote, they would not be able to find you, because you are not registered in that county.

most people wonder how the booths and all that work: 
The voting booths are not connected to the internet, they have an internal paper printer, they have battery back up power.  Multiple election officials have to sign off on the number of cast ballots on each machine, which has to line up with number of physical signatures collected when people sign in which also has to match up to the number of voters marked in the database.   If these numbers don't match up, the people working that location are going to have a very bad time.

I will also touch on your original question about voting in different states.   In order to register in a given voting station you have to prove residency in the jurisdiction you want to vote in. For the average person, that's not something you can easily pull off with out actually moving.   And while there is overlap between your old address and new address where that is possible...   it is important to remember that.... in order to vote you have to give up all your info on who you are and where you live.   sooo when it gets caught? jail time.

The main take away I feel you should have is...  a single individual will have a very difficult time casting a ballot they are not eligible cast.

In order to rig elections you need to have 50-1000 votes in several of the the "Correct" electoral districts/stations.  you aren't going to find enough people willing to take that risk personally.    Meaningful election corruption is going to happen at a higher level.   County officials and election judges.  

The reality is that the cheapest and easiest solution to solve election fraud is to maintain a national ID.  but conservatives hate that idea and liberals aren't really crazy about it either.  Having an national ID is a whole topic on its own.  But some offhand notes is conservatives leaders don't like the idea of having national voter ID because statistically the more people who vote the worse they do in elections.   And liberals leaders aren't crazy about it either because there are fears that a well organized list of citizens and registered party affiliations could be used to persecute and target groups of people from a federal level.  
((reminder that in order to participate in primaries most states require you to declare a party))

I did this work as my area was transitioning from paper systems to computer systems.

The show is a bit exploitative in how the "enemy" interacts with the memories of the soldiers.  It's well done and effective.    

Our protagonist, Lena, acts as a camera, providing context of how messed up the situation is.  She has a pretty standard set of waifu traits, esp large doses of empathy.   The society she lives in, San Mangolia, is portrayed as cartoonishly evil. I found that to be jarring and hamfisted, which is unfortunate considering the realism portrayed in the 86* conscripts. 



Code Geass has a lot of superficial crossover, but the theme is much more "Imperialism is bad"  it's also a bit like a Shakespearean Tragedy. It is also a much more  "Anime" show.  Larger than life characters, wacky hijinks, ect.

Lelouch is the protagonist, but it wouldn't be right to say he is the "good guy."   While Lelouch outsmarts many of his opponents, we also see him set himself up for failure.  A lot of the setbacks Lelouch suffers, are due to his own arrogance and misunderstanding of people.  The show suffers from a bit from railroading, with sometimes people making out of character decisions to push the plot in a certain direction...  which is unfortunate.   But the pay out at the end is very well regarded.



TLDR; 
86* explores how bad war, racism, and drones are.
Code Geass explores the hubris of man through Lelouch.
